rows.claim: M16,10 (ARC's 432-parameter example model) puts its largest logit on the position of the 2nd-largest of 10 standard Gaussian inputs this often.
rows.how: Monte Carlo with core.accuracy, float32 on GPU, seed 101. An independent 2^29-input run (benchmark.npz) gave 0.95313.

rows.claim: The five other trained 16-neuron, length-10 models in ARC's zoo (seeds 0-4) are less accurate than the example model.
Inputs whose 2nd-largest value is negative (at most one of the 10 is positive) are rare.
rows.how: Exact: P(at most one of 10 positive) = 11/2^10; sampled check with seed 404.

rows.claim: M16,10 is mostly wrong on inputs whose 2nd-largest value is negative.
rows.how: Monte Carlo, seed 404. These inputs hold 17.8% of all errors.

B.title: Errors are fuzzy comparisons

rows.claim: Most of M16,10's errors involve a close call: the share of errors in which some arriving input came within 0.1 of the running max or running 2nd max.
rows.how: Smallest arrival gap = min over steps t >= 1 of |x_t - running max| and |x_t - running 2nd max| (check3_gaps.py). Seed 202.

rows.claim: M16,10's accuracy on inputs whose smallest arrival gap is below 0.01 (a near-tie somewhere).
rows.how: As 2a.

rows.claim: M16,10's accuracy on inputs whose smallest arrival gap is between 0.1 and 0.2.
rows.how: As 2a.

rows.claim: M16,10's accuracy on inputs whose smallest arrival gap is at least 0.5 (no close call anywhere).
rows.how: As 2a.

B.notes: Review 1's 94% is its three bin shares rounded first and then added (0.36 + 0.32 + 0.26 = 0.94); unrounded, its own 2^22-input run (seed 5) gives 93.6%. The two old figures therefore agree. Review 1's '100% above 0.5' is the same rounding: accuracy is 99.95%.

C.title: Errors made at the last input

rows.claim: About half of M16,10's errors are made at the very last input: its running answer was right after 9 inputs and the 10th input broke it.
rows.how: Running answer after t inputs = argmax(W_oh h_t), right if on the running 2nd argmax s (padded slot s + 10 - t); last-input error = right after 9 inputs. Definition reconstructed (no script); seed 303.

rows.claim: Errors made at the last input, split by what the last input was: below the running 2nd max and taken for a new 2nd; below it, with the answer moving elsewhere (usually to the 3rd largest); a new max whose old position is not moved into the answer; a new 2nd whose slot is not written.
rows.how: As 3a; groups by the last input's rank among the first nine and the final answer. In the second group the answer is the 3rd largest in 67% of cases.

C.notes: Error start step (smallest t from 5 on after which the pointer stays wrong), share of errors: <=5: 18.2%, 6: 2.0%, 7: 3.8%, 8: 7.8%, 9: 17.7%, 10: 50.6%. Readouts before step 5 are unreliable, so earlier starts are lumped into '<=5'.

E.title: Top-k variance curve

rows.claim: Every input matters to M16,10: share of the variance of correctness explained by fixing the values and positions of the k largest inputs, for k = 1..9 (the rest resampled below them).
rows.n: 65,536 random anchor inputs x 256 resamples each, per k
rows.how: Between-anchor variance of the resampled accuracy, minus its sampling noise mean(p(1-p))/(R-1), over p(1-p). SE by bootstrap over anchors. Seed 505.

E.notes: Without the noise correction the shares are higher by about (1 - share)/256: 0.041, 0.244, 0.628, 0.769, 0.837, 0.882, 0.909, 0.937, 0.965.

F.title: Sensitivity by weight block

rows.claim: M16,10 is fragile in its six clean comparator neurons: multiplying each of the 36 recurrent weights among neurons 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8 by 1 + 0.01 N(0,1) drops accuracy from 0.953 to this spread over random draws.
rows.n: 48 noise draws; 16,777,216 common inputs per draw
rows.se: Monte Carlo SE per draw 0.0001; spread is between draws
rows.how: Weights x (1 + 0.01 N(0,1)); same inputs for every draw. Draw seed 6060, input seed 606.

rows.claim: The same 1% noise on M16,10's other weights costs less, but the clean neurons' input weights and outgoing weights still matter: the largest accuracy drop in any of 48 draws, per block of weights.
rows.value: clean neurons' input and outgoing weights: W_hh into the 10 others from clean neurons (60) 7.9 points; input weights of the clean neurons (6) 9.9 points; readout weights from clean neurons (60) 5.4 points. All other blocks: W_hh into clean neurons from the 10 others (60) 0.2; W_hh among the 10 other neurons (100) 1.9; input weights of the 10 others (10) 0.0; readout weights from the 10 others (100) 0.6
rows.n: 48 draws per block; 16,777,216 common inputs per draw
rows.how: As 6a, one block at a time; block split is this script's choice (the original was not recorded). Draw seeds 6061-6067.

F.notes: The old range 0.73-0.90 is one set of 12 draws; four sets of 12 give the ranges in row 6a, so quote the median and percentiles instead. Median drops per other block: W_hh into clean neurons from the 10 others (60) 0.0; W_hh into the 10 others from clean neurons (60) 1.1; W_hh among the 10 other neurons (100) 0.4; input weights of the clean neurons (6) 1.7; input weights of the 10 others (10) 0.0; readout weights from clean neurons (60) 2.0; readout weights from the 10 others (100) 0.2 points. Blocks that do not involve the clean neurons' input or outgoing weights never cost more than 1.9 points.

G.title: Five sensitive weights

rows.claim: A handful of M16,10's weights carry its sensitivity: the number of the 72 single +-1% changes to recurrent weights among the six clean neurons that cost more than 1 accuracy point, and the largest cost.
rows.se: paired SE 0.005 points or less; 0 changes within 3 SE of the 1-point line
rows.how: check7_sensitivity.py with 8x more inputs (seed 707). Paired SE = sd(c_new - c_base)/sqrt(n).

rows.claim: The costly single changes all involve the same few recurrent weights (row receives from column), and for some of them both +1% and -1% cost more than 1 point (a sharp optimum).
rows.old: [7,2], [2,2], [8,7], [1,7], [8,2]; both directions for the first four
rows.how: As 7a.

G.notes: Review 1 also reported n2's self-weight x 0.98 giving accuracy 0.80 when the max is 9 steps old and 0.93 when it just arrived; this run gives 0.801 and 0.935.

H.title: Noisy copies fail by position

rows.claim: Weight-noise copies of M16,10 fail by position: the share of the variance of correctness explained by the positions of the three largest inputs, in four degraded copies and in the base model.
rows.n: 8,388,608 common random inputs per model, 1,000 position cells
rows.old: 39-61% in three of four degraded copies, 10% in the fourth, 3% in the base model
rows.how: check6_noisy_anatomy.py's between-cell share, minus the sampling noise of the cell means (bias-corrected); SE from 16 independent batches. Copies are the four review 1 examined. Seed 808.

rows.claim: In the noisy copy mult0.02_8 (true accuracy 0.614), accuracy collapses when the 2nd largest input is 6 steps old (at position 3).
rows.n: 839,293 inputs with the 2nd max at position 3
rows.how: Accuracy by age of the 2nd max (age = 9 - position), check6_noisy_anatomy.py. Seed 808.

H.notes: Across all 96 noisy copies the share explained by the top-3 positions has median 0.20 and range 0.03-0.61 (SE per copy at most 0.0005); its correlation with true accuracy is -0.85. Naive (uncorrected) shares in the five review copies: mult0.005_5 0.057, mult0.01_3 0.425, mult0.01_8 0.103, mult0.02_8 0.610, mult0.02_16 0.393; base 0.028; the noise correction is below 0.001 at 2^23 inputs. The mild copy mult0.005_5 (true accuracy 0.932) gives 0.057.

rows.claim: M16,10's comparators are causal: zeroing any one of n7, n6, n1 or n8 in the final state drops accuracy on inputs whose last value is low (below the 3rd largest of the first nine) or a new 3rd to this range.
rows.n: 16,777,216 random inputs: 1,679,646 with a new-3rd last input, 11,743,316 with a low one
rows.how: Set h_10[j] = 0 before the readout; last-input type relative to the max, 2nd and 3rd of x_0..x_8. No original script; natural definition. Seed 1313. Per neuron (new 3rd / low): n7 31% / 21%; n6 43% / 25%; n1 43% / 21%; n8 39% / 20%.

rows.claim: Zeroing the max-jump neuron n4 in M16,10's final state breaks new maxima: accuracy on inputs whose last value is a new max.
rows.n: 1,678,457 inputs with a new-max last input
rows.how: As 13a.

I.title: Per-cell estimator

rows.claim: Review 1's per-cell estimator (each of the 720 top-3 position cells gets its mean input; accuracy = mean of Phi(margin/width)) misses the true accuracies of the 96 noisy copies by this root-mean-square error, overestimating on average.
rows.how: pilot_cells.py (k = 3, probit), order-statistic moments from 10^7 draws with seed 0; with seed 1 the RMSE moves by +0.00006. True accuracies from 2^29 inputs.

rows.claim: The per-cell estimator's error by noise level (weights multiplied by 1 + sigma N(0,1)).
rows.value: sigma 0.005: RMSE 0.016, bias +0.011; sigma 0.01: RMSE 0.059, bias +0.055; sigma 0.02: RMSE 0.097, bias +0.095
rows.how: As 9a.

rows.claim: The per-cell estimator is worth only a few dozen samples: the number of random samples whose expected RMSE equals its RMSE, against its cost in forward passes.
rows.value: 35 samples; cost 2,160 forward passes, at which sampling would have RMSE 0.0084
rows.how: Samples-equivalent = mean(p(1-p))/RMSE^2 over the 96 copies. Cost = 720 cells x 3 passes.

I.notes: On the base model the estimator gives 0.939 (true 0.953).

rows.claim: Keeping only the 2 largest inputs (all others set to zero, target still the original 2nd position) gives an accuracy Z_2 that misses the true accuracies of the 96 noisy copies by this RMSE, overestimating them.
rows.how: Exact, from the weights: exact_z2.py (angle intervals, first-index tie rule). Base model Z_2 = 0.9774.

rows.claim: Keeping only the 3 largest inputs (all others set to zero, target still the original 2nd position) gives an accuracy Z_3 that misses the true accuracies of the 96 noisy copies by this RMSE, overestimating them.
rows.how: Sampled, 33,554,432 inputs per copy (Monte Carlo SE of each Z_3 under 1e-4), seeds 3000+copy index. Base model Z_3 = 0.9490.

rows.claim: Keeping only the 4 largest inputs (all others set to zero, target still the original 2nd position) gives an accuracy Z_4 that misses the true accuracies of the 96 noisy copies by this RMSE, overestimating them.
rows.how: Sampled, 33,554,432 inputs per copy (Monte Carlo SE of each Z_4 under 1e-4), seeds 4000+copy index. Base model Z_4 = 0.9513.

K.title: Comparison thresholds by age

rows.claim: M16,10's new-max comparison is nearly unbiased at every age: the ratio x / stored max at which the network is equally likely to treat a new input as a new max or as a new 2nd, for stored maxima 0-8 steps old.
rows.n: 8,388,608 random inputs; 41,080-407,470 near-tie readouts per age, steps 5-10
rows.how: thresholds.py: logistic fit of the pointer's verdict (old max's slot vs newest slot) on x/max, using ratios within 0.15 of 1. Seed 1111.

rows.claim: In noisy copies of M16,10 the new-max threshold drifts with the age of the stored max: highest and lowest well-determined threshold over the 96 copies and ages 0-8.
rows.value: highest 1.29 (mult0.02_9, max 6 steps old); lowest 0.60 (mult0.02_7, 8 steps old), both outside the fitted ratios 0.85-1.15 and so extrapolated; 33 of 96 copies move more than 0.1 from 1 at some age
rows.n: 857 of 864 fits (96 copies x 9 ages) with SE <= 0.02; 8,388,608 inputs per copy
rows.old: climbs to 1.72 or sinks to 0.68 (copies not named)
rows.how: As 11a. The old 1.72 matches mult0.02_9 at age 7 (1.73, SE 0.24), an extrapolation far outside the fitted ratios 0.85-1.15; its thresholds by age 0-8 are 1.02, 1.01, 1.06, 1.07, 1.08, 1.17, 1.29, 1.73, 1.21.

K.notes: Thresholds beyond about 0.85 or 1.15 lie outside the ratios used in the fit and are extrapolations. The unfiltered extremes are 1.73 (mult0.02_9, age 7, SE 0.24) and -0.18 (mult0.02_19, age 8, SE 0.38). mult0.02_19's thresholds by age 0-8: 0.96, 0.94, 0.92, 0.87, 0.88, 0.87, 0.77, 0.45, -0.18. The base model's thresholds by age: 1.022, 1.000, 1.011, 1.002, 1.004, 1.005, 0.988, 0.999, 0.988.

rows.claim: On clear-cut ordinary steps (new input below 0.8 x the running 2nd max), M16,10's running answer stays on the 2nd max this often, by age of the 2nd max.
rows.n: 4,194,304 random inputs; 338,294-2,012,979 qualifying steps per age, steps 5-9
rows.how: fidelity.py: running answer argmax(W_oh h_t) right before the step and running 2nd max > 0; count steps where it shifts with the 2nd max. Seed 1212.

rows.claim: On the same steps, the noisy copy of M16,10 with the lowest fidelity at these ages (also the least accurate copy) loses its running answer when the 2nd max is 5-8 steps old: the share of steps it keeps it, at ages 5, 6, 7 and 8.
rows.how: As 12a, all 96 copies; mult0.02_9 has the lowest mean over ages 5-8. On fidelity.py's own inputs it gives 16%, 58%, 47%, 34%: the old range quoted only ages 5 and 8.
